headline: Tank farms are the least examined assets on a Gulf industrial site
deck: Storage tanks fail at the bottom, where nobody can see, and the consequence is environmental before it is operational.
excerpt: Tanks are one of the four equipment classes at STATIC Arabia. They hold the largest inventories on any industrial site, they are the cheapest major asset per cubic metre, and their dominant failure mode is invisible from outside.
content:
Every refinery, petrochemical complex, terminal and desalination plant has a tank farm, and it is the part of the site that attracts the least engineering attention relative to what it holds.

Tanks are the fourth equipment class at STATIC Arabia in Al Khobar, alongside pressure vessels, heat exchangers and pipelines. They are structurally simple — a cylindrical shell, a floor, a roof — and that simplicity is why they are cheap per cubic metre of storage and why they are easy to under-manage.

The dominant failure mode is the floor. Tank bottoms sit on a foundation, in contact with the product above and the ground below, and they corrode from both sides. Soil-side corrosion is driven by moisture, soil chemistry and the quality of the cathodic protection; product-side corrosion depends on what is stored and what water has settled out of it. Neither is visible during normal operation, because the floor is under the entire inventory.

That geometry is what makes tank integrity a scheduling problem rather than an inspection problem. A shell can be examined externally while the tank is in service. A floor cannot be assessed properly without taking the tank out, cleaning it and entering it, which means emptying a large inventory, managing the sludge, gas-freeing the space and losing the storage capacity for weeks. Operators therefore run tanks on longer inspection intervals than any other equipment class, and rely on indirect methods in between — acoustic emission testing, magnetic flux leakage on accessible areas, corrosion coupons and cathodic protection surveys.

The consequence of getting it wrong is not primarily an operational one. A leaking tank bottom releases product to ground, and the resulting liability is environmental and regulatory. That is a different risk profile to a vessel failure, and it is why tank integrity programmes tend to be driven by compliance frameworks rather than by production economics.

The Gulf adds its own conditions. High ambient temperatures increase vapour losses and drive the design towards floating roofs, whose seals are a maintenance item in their own right. Coastal sites combine humidity and chloride, which is an aggressive external corrosion environment for the shell and the roof. Ground conditions at reclaimed industrial sites raise settlement questions, and differential settlement distorts a tank in ways that stress the shell-to-floor weld.

The fabrication side is comfortably within regional capability. Field-erected storage tanks are built on site from rolled plate by specialist contractors, and the Gulf has an established population of them. Unlike thick-walled clad pressure vessels, this is not a category where the Kingdom has needed to import capability.

STATIC Arabia expects more than 5,000 professionals across the oil, gas, petrochemical, power and desalination sectors, and runs at Dhahran Expo until 10 September.
